The Marsh mongoose (Atilax paludinosus) is a medium-sized carnivoran inhabiting wetlands and riparian zones across sub-Saharan Africa, where its semi-aquatic lifestyle imposes distinct physiological constraints. Neonates emerge from the birth canal weighing approximately 100 grams [Wwb = approximately 100 grams], a modest but functional mass that allows the altricial pups to cling to the mother's fur during her aquatic foraging excursions. Field records indicate that under typical thermal conditions, the gestation period for this species lasts approximately 76 days [tg = approximately 76 days] at a core body temperature of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C], a duration that aligns with the energetic demands of producing a litter of two well-developed offspring. This relatively abbreviated gestation is consistent with patterns observed in other semi-aquatic herpestids, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid postnatal development over extended intrauterine growth. The predictable thermal environment of the nest, maintained near the maternal body temperature, likely facilitates synchronous organogenesis and may reduce the time required for neonatal thermoregulatory independence.

During the extended period of maternal dependence, the weaning process represents a critical nutritional transition for the developing offspring. Weaning, defined as the cessation of milk provisioning, occurs at 36 days since birth [tx = 36 days since birth] under the stable thermal conditions maintained within the natal burrow at 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C], marking the point at which the pups begin to consume solid prey items brought by the mother. At this juncture, the body mass of the juvenile has increased to approximately 550 grams [Wwx = approximately 550 grams], reflecting a growth rate that is sustained by the high lipid content of mongoose milk. This value, representing about one-sixth of the adult body mass, indicates that the post-weaning period must involve substantial further growth before the individuals can achieve full independence and begin hunting effectively. Comparative data from related species suggest that the duration of lactation may be influenced by local prey availability, with resource-rich environments allowing for earlier weaning and potentially larger litter sizes.

As the juveniles continue to develop, they undergo a prolonged period of somatic growth before reaching the threshold of reproductive capability. Female Marsh mongooses reach puberty at 255 days after birth [tp = 255 days after birth] when housed under controlled conditions simulating their natural thermal niche of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C], a milestone that coincides with the attainment of approximately two-thirds of the ultimate adult size. This relatively late onset of sexual maturation compared to other mongoose species of similar mass suggests a life-history trade-off in which extended growth periods may enhance competitive ability for territories along productive watercourses. Puberty in males is typically observed several weeks later than in females, a pattern that may relate to the metabolic costs associated with establishing dominance hierarchies. The timing of gonadal activation appears tightly linked to body condition, as females that fail to reach a critical mass threshold earlier may delay their first ovulation until the following breeding season.

The ultimate adult body size of the Marsh mongoose is approached gradually over the first year of life, with individuals attaining a maximum adult wet mass of 3300 grams [Wwi = 3300 grams]. This asymptotic mass, typical of a moderately sized herpestid, supports the species' locomotor demands for both terrestrial pursuit and aquatic propulsion. Reproductive output is correspondingly modest, with females producing two pups per litter [N_R_i = two pups per litter], and rates of reproduction are estimated at approximately 2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 litters per year] under favorable conditions, yielding a maximum annual reproductive rate that reflects the constraints of a semi-aquatic foraging niche. The combination of small litter size and relatively low frequency of breeding events is consistent with a K-selected life-history strategy in which parental investment per offspring is high, ensuring that each pup is adequately provisioned with aquatic prey items during the critical post-weaning period.

Longevity data for the Marsh mongoose suggest that individuals can achieve a maximum lifespan of approximately 20.8 years [am = approximately 20.8 years] when maintained under thermoneutral conditions at 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C], a value that positions this species among the longer-lived members of the Herpestidae family. This extended lifespan, coupled with the delayed onset of reproduction and modest annual fecundity, forms a life-history syndrome typical of mammals occupying stable, resource-rich wetland habitats. The comparatively slow pace of life is further reflected in the prolonged period required for pups to achieve nutritional independence, with the weaning process established at 36 days after birth [tx = 36 days after birth], after which the young continue to benefit from maternal guidance in prey capture techniques for several additional months at a temperature of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C]. Field observations indicate that survivorship of adults is high across most populations, although juvenile mortality during the first wet season can be substantial when flooding events inundate den sites.
